synopsis: The corpus identifies unseen people and light vehicles being run over by large machines as the deadliest documented collision pattern; smaller trucks and loaders particularly back over people [f2983, f11293, f2995]. The January 2005–June 2021 US evidence covers 13 haul-truck collisions, including three pedestrian collisions, but one summary describes the category counts as victims while another describes incidents and notes a double fatality, requiring care with denominators [f2992, f3073]. Pedestrians can legitimately be close to machines: workers 0.5–5 m behind them occupy a weak range for digital radar simulators, and near-zero relative speed can make time-to-collision misleading even at centimeter separation [f6220, f5328, f6214]. Protection must account for camera limitations involving posture and weather, cooperative systems requiring everyone to carry tags, and reported worker responses including tag removal, riskier positioning and requests for bypasses [f1638, f1670, f3034]. Regulatory acceptance emphasizes timely detection or warning and risk reduction; US 30 CFR 77.410 specifically requires enough sensing coverage for an endangered person to escape [f2397, f2084, f2444]. Virtual validation therefore needs site-specific pedestrian controls and separately validated human models, yet no validated off-road pedestrian-behaviour model was found and transfer of on-road detection and rare-event methods remains unproven or uncertain [f11499, f10350, f4356, f5406, f1114].

relations.note: Both identify unseen people or light vehicles being run over as the deadliest pattern.
Adds quarry context and contrasts reversing smaller machines with forward-moving haul trucks.
Both warn that near-zero relative speed makes time-to-collision unreliable at centimeter separation.
Both locate workers 0.5–5 m behind machines in digital radar simulators' weakest range.
Both link braking safety outcomes to site traffic rules and pedestrian controls.
Both report on-road pedestrian-in-the-loop VR and AR simulator precedents.
Clarifies that escape coverage must provide adequate time to leave the danger zone.
Identical category counts describe victims versus collisions; the latter also includes a double fatality.
Universal tagging requirements explain why untagged people fall outside cooperative sensing.
Reported tag removal provides a behavioral route to cooperative sensing's untagged-person limitation.
Missing validated pedestrian behavior models strengthens the need for separate human-model validation.
Posture-related detection limitations justify varying worker posture in the operating-domain taxonomy.
On-road hi-vis detection failures justify explicitly varying hi-vis presence in off-road tests.
Authorized ground-crew approaches exemplify legitimate close pedestrian presence.
Selective disabling of hazardous motions enables greater worker positioning freedom.
Adds exact boundary placement and deterministic reproducibility to controllable pedestrian assets.
Expands representative PPE surrogates into posture, hi-vis and occlusion variations.
Swing hazards demonstrate why protection must address hazardous motions beyond forward or reverse travel.
